title: The sound recording industry in the USA before 1950

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The story of the sound recording industry is mostly one of musical entertainment, although it also covers, for example, movies, television and even telephone answering systems. Thomas Edison's 1877 invention of the phonograph used a cylinder record which captured sound in a groove. Initially cylinders were made of tinfoil, and from the 1880s of wax. Unlike modern CDs, which are mostly of pre-recorded music, the phonograph was intended for speech — businessmen, lawyers and others could record themselves instead of using stenography (shorthand). However, business phonographs sold very poorly in the early years, and the phonograph industry was near bankruptcy. But in 1899, someone had the bright idea of building a phonograph operated by coins, pre-recording songs on cylinders, and putting the machines into amusement arcades — places of public entertainment which were popular at the time. People loved it. The various companies making phonographs quickly went into the cylinder business.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The industry aimed to produce a machine that would be cheap enough for people to buy, so that they could listen to pre-recorded music in their homes. This goal inspired an even more successful technology — the gramophone, which played a disc instead of a cylinder. Edison himself had considered it, but it was Emile Berliner who really developed it, in part because he realised it would be easy to stamp out large numbers of copies of disc recordings. In 1893 he began selling his cheap machine and seven-inch disc rubber records. In the early 1900s, Victor, the company that Berliner had set up, became one of the largest manufacturers of ‘talking machines’ and records.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cylinders declined in the face of the competition from discs, and before long there were three big companies in the USA producing discs and the machines to play them, while their subsidiaries dominated the market in Europe. They were selling about three million records a year by 1900 in the USA alone. The success of the record industry during the next two decades was phenomenal.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Unfortunately, the boom was drawing to a close. At first it seemed as if the culprit was excessive competition. Over 150 companies were making records or record players by about 1920, and they were all trying to undercut each other's prices. But the radio also acted as competition. During the 1920s, regular broadcasts began in many areas of the USA and Europe. Networks appeared, which linked together stations and broadcast programmes that were more spectacular than anything available on records. As a result, people bought fewer records. The downturn was disastrous. In the USA alone, the industry declined by about one half in the early 1920s, then stabilised for the rest of the decade. New technologies helped a little, but when the Great Depression came, in 1929, followed by a general downturn in consumer spending in the 1930s, many record companies went out of business.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Records continued to be sold in relatively small numbers. However, the 1930s also brought new opportunities. When the talking motion pictures arrived, for a few years they used discs for the soundtrack, before switching to a system that put it right on the edge of the film. In fact, the motion picture industry was where the real action was in the sound recording industry in the 1930s. Sales of recording equipment to motion picture producers financed research in improved technologies.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It was only in the late 1930s that the number of record discs sold began to climb back toward the highs of the early 1920s. This was partly due to the gradual recovery after the years of Depression, particularly in the USA. It was also due to the growing number of jukeboxes in use — machines that played a choice of recorded music when a coin was inserted. Jukeboxes consumed large numbers of records because these were usually changed every week or so. But the industry was still in trouble.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the early 1940s, during World War II, the entertainment industries were called into service to record music for the entertainment of troops stationed overseas. In the USA, the military sponsored the recording of both ordinary ten-inch discs (the standard consumer disc since about 1900) and ‘V-discs’ for this purpose. V-discs were large, 16-inch diameter discs made of flexible vinyl plastic. They were similar to the discs then being used by radio broadcasters to record programmes. They held 15 minutes or so of recorded sound and, unlike earlier discs, could be shipped overseas without fear of breaking.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: With the end of the war in 1945, many in the record industry hoped for a renewed interest in listening to music at home. Great technological changes were underway. During the 1930s and early 1940s, the German companies AEG and IG Farben had steadily improved the technology of magnetic recorders. These became the basis of remarkable studio tape recorders. The use of these recorders would soon revolutionise the making of records and movie soundtracks. What consumers saw in the stores was also changing. In 1948 and 1949, 45-rpm discs were introduced for singles, and long-playing records for albums. These new high fidelity discs marked a new era in home listening.
